questions.question: What are Java Streams and why do they exist? They are a declarative pipeline for processing collections — map, filter, reduce — that expresses what to compute, not how to iterate.
questions.title: Java Streams Fundamentals
questions.direct_answer: Java Streams (java.util.stream) is a declarative API for processing sequences of elements through a pipeline of operations — source, intermediate operations (filter, map, sorted), and a terminal operation (collect, reduce, forEach). They exist because the imperative for-loop way to transform, filter, and aggregate collections is verbose, error-prone, and hard to parallelize; a stream pipeline expresses the what (the computation) and lets the library handle the how (iteration, fusion, and even parallelism via parallelStream).

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand a stream as a lazy, single-use pipeline (source → intermediate → terminal) and can explain laziness, fusion, and why side effects break it.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Confusing a Stream with a collection ('it stores data'), or adding side effects (mutating outside) in a forEach, missing that streams are lazy and single-use.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Define a stream as a lazy, single-use pipeline of source→intermediate→terminal, explain that intermediate ops are lazy and fused, and that side effects in lambdas break the model — then name when parallelStream helps and when it hurts.

sections.title: Overview
sections.content: Java Streams (java.util.stream) is a declarative API for processing sequences of elements through a pipeline: a source (collection, array, generator), zero or more intermediate operations (filter, map, sorted, distinct), and one terminal operation (collect, reduce, forEach, count). They exist because the imperative for-loop style for transforming, filtering, and aggregating collections is verbose, repetitive, and hard to parallelize; a stream pipeline expresses what to compute and lets the library handle how to iterate, fuse operations, and even parallelize via parallelStream. Streams are not data structures — they don't store elements; they're a lazy pipeline that computes on demand.

sections.title: Core Concepts
sections.content: The core ideas: (1) the pipeline — source → intermediate ops → terminal op; (2) laziness — intermediate operations are not executed until a terminal operation runs, so a filter on an infinite stream is safe; (3) fusion — consecutive stateless intermediate ops (filter+map) are merged into a single pass at execution; (4) single-use — a stream can be consumed once; (5) stateful vs stateless ops — sorted/distinct are stateful (need buffering), filter/map are stateless; (6) side effects — lambdas should be stateless and side-effect-free; mutating external state in forEach is the classic bug; (7) parallelStream — uses the ForkJoinPool; helps for CPU-bound, large, stateless pipelines, hurts for small or I/O-bound ones due to overhead and contention.

sections.title: A stream pipeline: lazy, fused, single-use
Trade-offs & When It Matters
sections.content: The central tension is readability versus control: a stream pipeline is often clearer than a for-loop, but it hides iteration, making debugging (no stack-trace into a lambda) and early-exit semantics (break/continue) harder. A second tension: parallelStream promises free parallelism but adds ForkJoinPool overhead and contention — it helps only for large, CPU-bound, stateless pipelines and can be slower or non-deterministic for small or I/O-bound ones. The third: streams are lazy, so side effects in intermediate lambdas are especially dangerous — they may run zero times (if terminal short-circuits) or in unexpected order, producing silent bugs.

sections.title: Key Takeaways
items: A Stream is a lazy, single-use pipeline (source → intermediate → terminal), not a data structure — it stores nothing.
Intermediate ops are lazy and fused: filter+map run as one pass at terminal-op time, with no intermediate collection.
Stateful ops (sorted, distinct) need to buffer elements; stateless ops (filter, map) don't.
A stream is consumed once — reusing it after a terminal op throws IllegalStateException.
Side effects in lambdas (mutating external state in forEach) break the model; use collect for accumulation.
parallelStream helps only for large, CPU-bound, stateless pipelines; for small or I/O-bound ones its ForkJoinPool overhead and contention make it slower or non-deterministic.

sections.title: Spoken Answer
sections.content: Java Streams are a declarative API for processing collections through a pipeline — a source, intermediate operations like filter and map, and a terminal operation like collect or reduce — and they exist because the imperative for-loop style is verbose and hard to parallelize. The mental model I stress is that a stream is a lazy, single-use pipeline, not a data structure: it stores nothing. The intermediate operations are lazy — nothing executes until a terminal operation runs — and they're fused, so filter and map run as a single pass with no intermediate collection. A stream is consumed once; reusing it after a terminal throws an IllegalStateException. The bugs I see most are side effects — people mutating external state in a forEach instead of using collect — and parallelStream, which people reach for thinking it's free parallelism, but it only helps for large, CPU-bound, stateless pipelines; for small or I/O-bound work its ForkJoinPool overhead and contention make it slower or non-deterministic.

questions.question: What is a lambda expression in Java? How does it compile and what are the scoping rules?
questions.title: Lambda Expressions in Java — Syntax, Scoping, and `invokedynamic`
questions.direct_answer: A **lambda expression** (Java 8+) is a concise way to represent an instance of a **functional interface** — an interface with exactly one abstract method. Syntax: `(params) -> expression` or `(params) -> { statements; }`. The compiler infers the lambda's target type from context (e.g., `Predicate<String>`, `Runnable`, `Function<T, R>`). At runtime, lambdas are **not** desugared into anonymous classes; they're compiled to **`invokedynamic`** instructions that delegate to **`LambdaMetafactory`**, which lazily generates the interface implementation — typically faster startup, smaller bytecode, and no class file per lambda. Scoping rules: lambdas have **lexical scope** (no separate `this` — `this` refers to the enclosing class instance), can read **effectively final local variables** from the enclosing scope (the variable can't be reassigned), and freely access enclosing instance and static fields. Unlike anonymous classes, lambdas don't create a new scope for `this` and don't generate a new `.class` file per use site. The end result: shorter, more readable code for callbacks, comparators, stream operations, event handlers — anywhere you'd previously use an anonymous inner class implementing a single-method interface.

sections.title: Syntax — The Forms a Lambda Can Take
Lambda vs Anonymous Class — Key Differences
sections.content:
Lambdas look like syntactic sugar for anonymous classes, but they're fundamentally different.

```java
// Anonymous class
Runnable r1 = new Runnable() {
    @Override
    public void run() {
        System.out.println(this);  // Prints anonymous class instance
    }
};

// Lambda
Runnable r2 = () -> System.out.println(this);  // Prints enclosing class instance (e.g., MyService@abc)
```

**Differences**:

| Aspect | Anonymous class | Lambda |
|---|---|---|
| `this` reference | The anonymous instance | Enclosing class instance |
| New class file | Yes (`Outer$1.class`) | No (generated lazily by `LambdaMetafactory`) |
| Compilation output | New class with constructor | `invokedynamic` instruction |
| Captured variables | Compiler copies into synthetic fields | Same, but lazy class generation |
| Can extend a class | Yes (anonymous subclass) | No — only functional interfaces |
| Multiple methods | Yes | No — single-abstract-method only |
| Memory per call site | One instance (shared) or new per call | Zero for non-capturing (cached); one per capture for capturing |
| Startup cost | Higher (class loaded eagerly) | Lower (class generated on first call) |

**Practical implications**:
- Use a **lambda** for callbacks and stream operations — cleaner, faster startup, no surprise `this`.
- Use an **anonymous class** when you need to extend a non-functional interface, override multiple methods, or capture `this` of the inner type.
- A lambda over `Comparator<T>` is essentially the same as `new Comparator<T>() { compare(...) }` — shorter and faster.

sections.title: What Lambdas Compile To — invokedynamic and LambdaMetafactory
sections.content:
When `javac` encounters a lambda, it does **not** generate an anonymous class file. Instead it emits:

1. A **synthetic static method** in the enclosing class containing the lambda body.
2. An **`invokedynamic` instruction** at the use site, with `LambdaMetafactory.metafactory` as the bootstrap method.

First time the `invokedynamic` site executes, the JVM calls `LambdaMetafactory`, which:
- Generates a small class implementing the target functional interface.
- The generated class delegates to the synthetic static method (or holds captured values).
- Caches the call site so subsequent invocations skip generation.

**Bytecode example** (conceptual):
```
// Original
Runnable r = () -> System.out.println("hi");

// Compiled to:
//  - synthetic static method: lambda$0()V { System.out.println("hi"); }
//  - invokedynamic at use site:
//      invokedynamic Runnable.run() => LambdaMetafactory.metafactory(...)
//                                       targeting lambda$0
```

**Why this matters**:
- **No class file per lambda** — smaller JARs, faster classpath scans, less JIT load.
- **Lazy class generation** — lambdas you never invoke cost nothing.
- **Non-capturing lambdas reuse a single instance** — the call site caches it. `() -> System.out.println("hi")` allocates zero objects on subsequent calls.
- **Capturing lambdas allocate a new instance per capture** — because each captured value is different.

**Performance implications**:
- Cold start: lambdas are slightly slower the first time (class generation).
- Hot path: lambdas match or beat anonymous classes (cached call site, fewer indirections).
- For tight loops, prefer non-capturing lambdas — zero allocation.
- Method references (`User::getName`) are usually as fast as direct calls thanks to JIT.

sections.title: Variable Capture and Effectively Final
Practical Lambda Patterns
When to Use Lambdas vs Alternatives
sections.content:
**Use lambdas when**:
- Implementing a single-abstract-method (functional) interface inline.
- Stream operations, comparators, event handlers, callbacks.
- The body is a few lines or a single method call (use a **method reference** if it's just a method call).
- Code reads more clearly than the equivalent anonymous class.

**Don't use lambdas when**:
- The body is more than ~5–10 lines — extract a method.
- You need to capture `this` of the inner type (use anonymous class).
- You need to override multiple methods (use anonymous or named class).
- You're implementing a non-functional interface.
- The lambda involves complex business logic that deserves a name and unit tests.

**Lambda vs method reference**:
- Prefer method references when they read more clearly: `User::getName` over `u -> u.getName()`.
- Use a lambda when you need parameter manipulation or multiple operations.
- Method references can be slightly faster (one fewer indirection in some cases).

**Performance considerations**:
- Non-capturing lambdas: zero allocation per use after first call.
- Capturing lambdas: one allocation per call (carries captured values).
- Avoid creating capturing lambdas in hot loops; lift them out if possible.
- For very hot paths, profile to confirm — most JIT compilers handle lambdas well.

**Common pitfalls**:
- **Forgetting effectively-final** — compile error; use a wrapper if you really need mutation.
- **Lambda `this` confusion** — it's the outer class's `this`, not the lambda's. If you need the lambda instance, pass it as a parameter.
- **Checked exceptions** — standard functional interfaces don't declare them. Either wrap in `RuntimeException`, define a custom functional interface, or use a sneaky-throw helper.
- **Long lambdas** — extract to a method or named class for readability.
- **Capturing mutable state in parallel streams** — race conditions; use a collector instead.

- **Lambda**: instance of a functional interface (single-abstract-method).
- **Syntax**: `(params) -> expression` or `(params) -> { statements; }`.
- **Target typing**: compiler infers the functional interface from context.
- **Compiles to `invokedynamic` + `LambdaMetafactory`** — not anonymous classes.
- **No class file per lambda** — generated lazily on first use.
- **Non-capturing lambdas**: zero allocation after first call (cached).
- **Capturing lambdas**: one allocation per capture.
- **`this` is lexical** — refers to the enclosing class instance.
- **Captured local variables must be effectively final** — compiler-enforced for clarity.
- **Instance/static fields**: freely accessible (and mutable, though usually a code smell).
- **Workaround for mutable capture**: `AtomicReference`/`AtomicInteger` or one-element array.
- **Differs from anonymous class**: different `this`, no separate class file, can't extend non-functional interfaces, can't override multiple methods.
- **Method references** (`User::getName`) are often clearer than equivalent lambdas.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
A lambda expression is a concise way to write an instance of a functional interface — an interface with exactly one abstract method. Java 8 introduced them to make callbacks, comparators, and stream operations far more readable than anonymous inner classes.

**Syntax**
- `(params) -> expression` for single-expression bodies
- `(params) -> { statements; }` for block bodies
- One parameter? parens optional: `s -> s.length()`
- No parameters? `() -> doSomething()`
- Java 11+: `var` in parameters allows annotations: `(@NonNull var s) -> ...`

**Target typing**
- The compiler infers the lambda's type from context
- The lambda's signature must match the functional interface's single abstract method
- Same lambda, different context: `s -> s.length()` is `Function<String, Integer>` here, `ToIntFunction<String>` there

**Lambda vs anonymous class — they're not the same**
- `this` in a lambda refers to the **enclosing class** instance; in an anonymous class it refers to the inner instance
- No new class file per lambda; anonymous classes generate `Outer$1.class`
- Lambdas compile to `invokedynamic` instructions backed by `LambdaMetafactory`
- Lambdas are lazy: the implementation class is generated on first use
- Non-capturing lambdas are cached — zero allocation per call
- Capturing lambdas allocate one instance per capture

**The `invokedynamic` mechanism**
- `javac` extracts the lambda body into a synthetic static method
- At the use site, emits `invokedynamic` with `LambdaMetafactory.metafactory` as the bootstrap
- First execution: JVM generates a class implementing the functional interface, caches the call site
- Subsequent calls: cached, fast
- Result: smaller JARs, faster startup, better JIT optimization

**Variable capture rules**

**1. Effectively final local variables only**
- Either declared `final` or never reassigned after initialization
- Compile error if you try to reassign a captured local
- Why: lambdas may run later on different threads; capture-by-value avoids race conditions

**2. Instance and static fields**
- Freely readable and writable from a lambda
- But mutating shared state in parallel streams is a race condition; use collectors

**3. Workaround for mutable capture**
- `AtomicInteger` for counters: `counter.incrementAndGet()`
- One-element array: `int[] counter = {0};` then `counter[0]++`
- Both are code smells — prefer immutable patterns

**4. `this` is lexical**
- Always refers to the enclosing class instance
- Not the lambda itself; lambdas don't have their own `this`

**When to use lambdas**
- Stream operations, comparators, event handlers, callbacks
- Strategy pattern with `Map<String, Function<...>>`
- Functional builders, lazy initialization
- Body fits in a few lines; longer bodies should be extracted methods

**When NOT to use lambdas**
- Body is more than ~5–10 lines (extract a method)
- Need to override multiple methods or extend a class (use anonymous or named class)
- Need the inner instance's `this` (use anonymous class)
- Complex business logic that deserves a name and unit tests

**Common pitfalls**
- **Effectively-final compile error** — don't reassign captured locals; use a wrapper if you really need mutation
- **`this` confusion** — lambda `this` is the outer class, not the lambda
- **Checked exceptions** — standard functional interfaces don't declare them; wrap in `RuntimeException`, define a custom interface, or use a sneaky-throw helper
- **Capturing mutable state in parallel streams** — race conditions; use collectors

**Recommendation:** Use lambdas as the **default** for any single-method interface implementation — they're cleaner, faster to start (lazy class generation), and play well with the JIT. Reach for **method references** (`User::getName`) when the lambda is just calling an existing method; they read better and are sometimes marginally faster. Reserve **anonymous classes** for the cases lambdas can't handle: extending a class, overriding multiple methods, or needing the inner instance's `this`. Keep lambda bodies short — if it's longer than a few lines, extract a named method; you gain a stack-trace-friendly symbol and a test target. Always remember **`this` is lexical** in a lambda and **captured locals must be effectively final** — these two rules catch most newcomers and are the source of subtle bugs in async code.

questions.question: What is a functional interface in Java? When should you use `@FunctionalInterface`?
questions.title: Functional Interfaces in Java — Single Abstract Method Contracts
questions.direct_answer: A **functional interface** is any interface with **exactly one abstract method (SAM)** — it can have any number of `default`, `static`, and `private` methods, plus methods inherited from `Object` (which don't count toward the SAM rule). The single abstract method makes the interface eligible as the **target type for a lambda expression** or **method reference**. The **`@FunctionalInterface`** annotation is **optional** but recommended on intentionally functional interfaces — it makes the compiler enforce the SAM constraint, so accidentally adding a second abstract method (now or later) becomes a compile error rather than a silent breaking change. Standard library examples: `Runnable` (`void run()`), `Callable<V>` (`V call() throws Exception`), `Comparator<T>` (`int compare(T, T)`), and the `java.util.function` family (`Function<T,R>`, `Consumer<T>`, `Supplier<T>`, `Predicate<T>`, `BiFunction`, etc.). Define a custom one when no standard interface fits — for example, when you need to declare a checked exception or use more than two parameters. Common rule: keep functional interfaces small and focused; if you find yourself adding methods, you've probably outgrown the pattern.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking @FunctionalInterface is required for lambda compatibility (it's not). Confusing 'one abstract method' with 'one method' (default/static methods don't count). Defining custom interfaces when a standard one would do
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that Object methods (equals, hashCode, toString) don't count toward SAM, discuss the value of @FunctionalInterface for API stability, and know when to use checked-exception variants

sections.title: The SAM Rule — Single Abstract Method
@FunctionalInterface — Optional but Recommended
Standard Functional Interfaces from `java.util.function`
sections.content:
Java 8 added a rich library of generic functional interfaces — use them before defining your own.

**Core four**:
```java
Function<T, R>     // T -> R           e.g., String::length
Predicate<T>       // T -> boolean     e.g., String::isEmpty
Consumer<T>        // T -> void        e.g., System.out::println
Supplier<T>        // () -> T          e.g., () -> new ArrayList<>()
```

**Two-argument variants**:
```java
BiFunction<T, U, R>   // (T, U) -> R
BiPredicate<T, U>     // (T, U) -> boolean
BiConsumer<T, U>      // (T, U) -> void
```

**Same-type operators** (avoid generic noise):
```java
UnaryOperator<T>      // T -> T   (extends Function<T, T>)
BinaryOperator<T>     // (T, T) -> T   (extends BiFunction<T, T, T>)
```

**Primitive specializations** (avoid boxing in hot paths):
```java
IntFunction<R>, LongFunction<R>, DoubleFunction<R>
ToIntFunction<T>, ToLongFunction<T>, ToDoubleFunction<T>
IntPredicate, LongPredicate, DoublePredicate
IntConsumer, LongConsumer, DoubleConsumer
IntSupplier, LongSupplier, DoubleSupplier
IntUnaryOperator, IntBinaryOperator
// And many more combinations
```

**Pre-existing functional interfaces** (work seamlessly with lambdas):
```java
Runnable             // () -> void  (but throws nothing)
Callable<V>          // () -> V throws Exception
Comparator<T>        // (T, T) -> int
Iterable<T>.forEach (Consumer)
Thread, ThreadFactory, etc.
```

**Default methods on standard interfaces** — the real power:
```java
Predicate<User> isActive = User::isActive;
Predicate<User> isAdmin = u -> u.getRole() == Role.ADMIN;
Predicate<User> isActiveAdmin = isActive.and(isAdmin);  // composed
Predicate<User> notActive = isActive.negate();

Function<String, String> trim = String::trim;
Function<String, String> upper = String::toUpperCase;
Function<String, String> trimUpper = trim.andThen(upper);
```

sections.title: When to Define a Custom Functional Interface
Default and Static Methods — Why They Matter
Design Trade-offs and Pitfalls
sections.content:
**Strengths**:
- Lambdas + functional interfaces eliminate the verbosity of anonymous classes.
- Standard library covers most needs (`Function`, `Consumer`, `Predicate`, `Supplier`).
- Default methods enable composition without bloating the SAM contract.
- `@FunctionalInterface` makes the contract enforceable.

**Pitfalls**:
- **Don't confuse 'one abstract method' with 'one method'** — default/static methods don't count.
- **Object methods don't count** — explicitly redeclaring `equals` doesn't break the SAM rule.
- **Checked exceptions** — standard interfaces don't declare them; either use a custom interface, wrap in `RuntimeException`, or use a sneaky-throw helper.
- **Boxing overhead** — `Function<Integer, Integer>` boxes; use `IntUnaryOperator` instead for tight loops.
- **Overly clever interfaces** — a functional interface with 5 default methods is harder to read than a small abstract class. If you're approaching that, consider a regular interface or class.
- **Over-customizing** — don't define `MyFunction<T, R>` when `Function<T, R>` works. Reserve custom names for domain semantics.

**When NOT to make something a functional interface**:
- Multiple semantically distinct operations — keep them as regular interfaces.
- Operations that are logically tied to state — use a class.
- Anything where the lambda body would be > ~10 lines — named methods are clearer.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Functional interface**: exactly one abstract method (SAM).
- **Default, static, private, and Object methods don't count** toward the SAM.
- **`@FunctionalInterface`** is optional but recommended — enforces the SAM at compile time.
- **Eligible as lambda target**: any interface meeting the SAM rule.
- **Standard library** in `java.util.function`: `Function`, `Consumer`, `Supplier`, `Predicate`, `BiFunction`, plus primitive variants.
- **Pre-existing**: `Runnable`, `Callable`, `Comparator`, etc.
- **Default methods** on standard interfaces enable composition: `Function.andThen`, `Predicate.and`, `Comparator.thenComparing`.
- **Define a custom interface** when you need: checked exceptions, more than two parameters, domain-meaningful name, or domain-specific default methods.
- **Avoid boxing** in hot paths — use `IntFunction`, `ToIntFunction`, etc.
- **Pitfalls**: confusing one method with one abstract method, defining custom interfaces when standard ones work, overusing default methods.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
A **functional interface** is any interface with **exactly one abstract method** — the SAM rule. That's the only requirement. It can have any number of `default`, `static`, `private` (Java 9+), and `Object`-overriding methods, none of which count toward the SAM.

**The SAM rule — what counts and what doesn't**

Counts:
- Abstract methods declared by the interface

Doesn't count:
- `default` methods (have implementation)
- `static` methods (belong to the interface)
- `private` methods (helpers, Java 9+)
- Overrides of `Object` methods (`equals`, `hashCode`, `toString`)

This is why `Comparator` is a functional interface despite having many methods — only `compare(T, T)` is abstract.

**`@FunctionalInterface` annotation**

- **Optional** — the compiler treats SAM-compliant interfaces as functional whether you annotate or not
- **Recommended** for intentionally functional interfaces:
  - Documents intent
  - Compiler enforces the SAM rule — adding a second abstract method becomes a compile error
  - Catches the mistake at the interface, not at every lambda use site
- **Don't annotate** interfaces that happen to be SAM but aren't meant to be functional (like `Closeable`)

**Standard library — use these first**

**Core four** in `java.util.function`:
- `Function<T, R>` — transforms T to R
- `Predicate<T>` — returns boolean
- `Consumer<T>` — returns void
- `Supplier<T>` — no input, returns T

**Two-argument variants**: `BiFunction`, `BiPredicate`, `BiConsumer`

**Same-type operators**: `UnaryOperator<T>`, `BinaryOperator<T>`

**Primitive specializations** (avoid boxing): `IntFunction<R>`, `ToIntFunction<T>`, `IntPredicate`, etc.

**Pre-existing functional interfaces**: `Runnable`, `Callable`, `Comparator` — work seamlessly with lambdas.

**Default methods enable composition**
- `Function.andThen`, `Function.compose`, `Function.identity()`
- `Predicate.and`, `or`, `negate`, `Predicate.not(...)` (Java 11+)
- `Comparator.comparing`, `thenComparing`, `reversed`
- This is why functional interfaces with one abstract method can still expose a rich API

**When to define a custom functional interface**

**1. Need a checked exception**
- `@FunctionalInterface interface ThrowingFunction<T, R> { R apply(T t) throws Exception; }`
- Standard `Function` doesn't declare exceptions — forces lambda authors to wrap

**2. More than two parameters**
- Standard library stops at `Bi*` — define a `TriFunction` if you need three

**3. Domain-meaningful name**
- `RetryPolicy` reads better than `BiPredicate<Integer, Throwable>`
- Even if structurally equivalent, the name documents intent at every use site

**4. Domain-specific default methods**
- Add convenience methods like `serializeAll(collection)` that build on the SAM

**Pitfalls**
- **Confusing 'one method' with 'one abstract method'** — defaults and statics don't count
- **Boxing overhead** — `Function<Integer, Integer>` boxes; use `IntUnaryOperator` in hot paths
- **Over-customizing** — don't define `MyFunction` when `Function` works
- **Overly clever interfaces** — if a functional interface has 5+ default methods, consider a regular interface or abstract class
- **Forgetting `@FunctionalInterface`** on intentionally functional interfaces — a future maintainer might break the contract

**Recommendation:** Always start by checking if a **standard** `java.util.function` interface fits — 90% of the time it does. Add **`@FunctionalInterface`** to any interface you intentionally design for lambda use; it costs nothing and prevents accidental breakage. Define a **custom interface** only when you have a specific reason: a checked exception, more than two parameters, a domain-meaningful name, or domain-specific defaults. Use **primitive specializations** (`IntFunction`, `ToIntFunction`) in performance-sensitive paths to avoid boxing. Lean on **default methods** for composition — they're the secret ingredient that makes Java's functional interfaces ergonomic. The pattern is: keep the SAM small and abstract, layer convenience as defaults, use the annotation as a guardrail.

The Standard Functional Interfaces
sections.content:
| Interface | Input → Output | Example Use |
|---|---|---|
| `Function<T, R>` | T → R | `String::length` for `Function<String, Integer>` |
| `BiFunction<T, U, R>` | (T, U) → R | `Integer::sum` for `BiFunction<Integer, Integer, Integer>` |
| `Predicate<T>` | T → boolean | `String::isEmpty` for `Predicate<String>` |
| `BiPredicate<T, U>` | (T, U) → boolean | `(a, b) -> a.equals(b)` |
| `Consumer<T>` | T → void | `System.out::println` for `Consumer<String>` |
| `BiConsumer<T, U>` | (T, U) → void | `map::put` for `BiConsumer<K, V>` |
| `Supplier<T>` | nothing → T | `LocalDateTime::now` for `Supplier<LocalDateTime>` |
| `UnaryOperator<T>` | T → T | `String::toUpperCase` for `UnaryOperator<String>` |
| `BinaryOperator<T>` | (T, T) → T | `Integer::max` for `BinaryOperator<Integer>` |

**Primitive specializations** (avoid boxing):

| Interface | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `IntFunction<R>`, `LongFunction<R>`, `DoubleFunction<R>` | primitive → R |
| `ToIntFunction<T>`, `ToLongFunction<T>`, `ToDoubleFunction<T>` | T → primitive |
| `IntPredicate`, `LongPredicate`, `DoublePredicate` | primitive → boolean |
| `IntConsumer`, `LongConsumer`, `DoubleConsumer` | primitive → void |
| `IntSupplier`, `LongSupplier`, `DoubleSupplier`, `BooleanSupplier` | nothing → primitive |
| `IntUnaryOperator`, `IntBinaryOperator`, ... | primitive arithmetic |

**Rule**: when your lambda handles primitives, use the specialization — `IntStream` uses `IntFunction` and `IntPredicate`, which means no `int → Integer` boxing on every element. For a stream over 1 million `int`s, this is 1 million allocations saved.

sections.title: Idiomatic Lambda Usage and Composition
Under the Hood — invokedynamic and LambdaMetafactory
sections.content:
A common misconception: lambdas are compiled to anonymous inner classes. They are **not**. The compilation model is different and more efficient.

**Pre-Java 8 anonymous class**:
- Compiles to a separate `.class` file — `OuterClass$1.class`
- `.class` file loaded the first time through `ClassLoader`
- Each `new` statement allocates a new instance

**Java 8+ lambda**:
- Compiles to an **`invokedynamic`** bytecode instruction
- At first execution, the JVM calls **`LambdaMetafactory.metafactory(...)`** passing the target functional interface type, the lambda's bootstrap method handle, and the captured parameters
- `LambdaMetafactory` generates a lightweight class via `java.lang.invoke` and caches it
- Subsequent executions reuse the cached class

**Key performance implications**:

**1. Stateless lambdas are singletons**

```java
// Lambda captures no local state — one instance exists forever
Supplier<Integer> answer = () -> 42;
Supplier<Integer> another = () -> 42;
// answer == another is NOT guaranteed, but they may share instance
// Each call to get() returns the same result with zero allocation
```

**2. Capturing lambdas allocate per unique capture**

```java
for (int i = 0; i < 1000; i++) {
    int finalI = i;
    submit(() -> process(finalI));  // each lambda captures different finalI
}
// Allocates 1000 different lambda instances
```

**3. The JIT can inline lambda bodies**

Because the `invokedynamic` call site is stable after the first invocation, the JIT treats it like a direct call — the lambda body is inlined into the caller. This is why `stream.map(x -> x * 2)` can match or beat the speed of a hand-written `for` loop after JIT warmup.

**4. No `.class` file per lambda**

Old anonymous-class compilation produced `OuterClass$1.class`, `OuterClass$2.class`, etc. — your JAR grew with every lambda. `invokedynamic` generates classes at runtime from a template; the JAR stays small.

**Benchmark reference** (JMH, 1 billion calls):

```
Anonymous class invocation:  2,800 ms
Lambda invocation:           2,100 ms
Method reference:            2,100 ms
Direct method call:          2,050 ms
```

Lambdas and method references are essentially as fast as direct calls on a hot JIT path.

sections.title: When Lambdas Help and When They Don't
sections.content:
**Lambdas are great for**:

- **Single-line behavior** as argument: `stream.filter(x -> x > 0)`, `Collections.sort(list, byLength)`
- **Event handlers**: `button.addActionListener(e -> doSomething())`
- **Functional composition**: chaining `Function`s, `Predicate`s
- **Strategy pattern**: pass different behaviors without subclass hierarchies
- **Callbacks**: `CompletableFuture.thenApply(result -> transform(result))`

**Lambdas are worse than alternatives for**:

- **Complex logic** — if the body is longer than ~5 lines, extract to a named method and use a method reference or direct call. Lambdas discourage good naming.
- **Checked exceptions** — standard `Function` doesn't declare `throws`. `stream.map(Files::readString)` won't compile because `readString` throws `IOException`. Workarounds: wrap in try-catch (ugly), use a custom `@FunctionalInterface ThrowingFunction` (some ceremony), or use a library like `jOOλ` or `Vavr`.
- **Recursion** — a lambda can't refer to itself directly (you can't name `this` as the lambda). Workarounds use `UnaryOperator` stored in a variable, or a method reference.
- **Multiple overloads / target-type ambiguity** — when two overloaded methods both accept functional interfaces, the compiler may reject the lambda as ambiguous. Cast or use a named variable.
- **Debugging** — stack traces with lambdas show synthetic names like `lambda$0`, harder to read than anonymous class names.

**Effectively final capture**:

Local variables used inside a lambda must be **effectively final** — assigned once and never changed. This is because lambdas may outlive the enclosing method (stored in fields, submitted to executors, etc.), and mutable captured state would require synchronization.

```java
String prefix = "[log] ";
Consumer<String> logger = msg -> System.out.println(prefix + msg);
// OK — prefix never reassigned

prefix = "[LOG] ";   // COMPILE ERROR if above lambda is present: 'prefix' must be effectively final
```

**For mutation**, prefer `AtomicReference`, arrays, or — better — redesign to avoid the need.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
A **functional interface** is any interface with exactly one abstract method — `Runnable`, `Comparator`, `Callable`, or the ones from `java.util.function`. The `@FunctionalInterface` annotation is a compile-time safeguard against accidentally adding a second abstract method.

A **lambda** is compact syntax for implementing a functional interface: `(params) -> body`. **Target typing** infers which interface the lambda implements from the context — the variable type, parameter type, or return type.

The **five standard functional interfaces** cover most use cases. **`Function<T, R>`** — T in, R out. **`Predicate<T>`** — T in, boolean out. **`Consumer<T>`** — T in, void. **`Supplier<T>`** — nothing in, T out. **`UnaryOperator<T>`** and **`BinaryOperator<T>`** for same-type transformations. Plus `Bi-` versions for two arguments, and primitive specializations like `IntFunction`, `ToIntFunction`, `IntPredicate` that avoid boxing overhead — critical in hot loops over millions of elements.

**Composition is built in** via default methods. `function.andThen(g)` applies `function` then `g`. `predicate.and(other)` combines two predicates. `consumer.andThen(next)` chains side effects.

**Under the hood**, lambdas are **not compiled to anonymous classes**, despite the common misconception. The compiler emits an **`invokedynamic`** instruction that calls `LambdaMetafactory` at runtime. The metafactory generates a lightweight class via `java.lang.invoke` and caches it. Consequences: **stateless lambdas are singletons** — `() -> 42` allocates once ever — and the **JIT inlines lambda bodies** into the call site, so on a hot path lambdas match direct-call speed.

**Effectively final** captured variables — locals referenced inside a lambda cannot be reassigned. The restriction exists because lambdas may outlive the enclosing method, and mutable captured state would need synchronization.

The rule I give junior engineers: **use method references when the body is just one method call** — `String::toUpperCase` over `s -> s.toUpperCase()` — and **extract to a named method when the body grows past 5 lines**. Lambdas make intent clear for one-liners but hurt readability for longer logic.

questions.title: Predicate, Function, Consumer, Supplier — Java's Core Functional Interfaces
questions.direct_answer: These are the **four core functional interfaces** in `java.util.function`, each modeling a fundamental shape of computation: **`Function<T, R>`** transforms one value to another (`apply`); **`Predicate<T>`** tests a value and returns `boolean` (`test`); **`Consumer<T>`** accepts a value and does something with no return (`accept`); **`Supplier<T>`** takes nothing and produces a value (`get`). They also have **two-argument variants** (`BiFunction`, `BiPredicate`, `BiConsumer`) and **primitive specializations** (`IntFunction`, `ToIntFunction`, `IntPredicate`, `IntConsumer`, `IntSupplier`) to avoid boxing in hot paths. The mental model: think of any computation as one of these four shapes, pick the matching interface, and chain combinators when you need composition. Knowing this vocabulary fluently is what makes Stream API code idiomatic.

sections.title: The Four Shapes of Computation
sections.content:
Every computation can be classified by its inputs and outputs. The four core interfaces capture the most common shapes:

| Interface | Shape | Method | Stream usage |
|---|---|---|---|
| `Function<T, R>` | T → R (transform) | `R apply(T)` | `map(...)` |
| `Predicate<T>` | T → boolean (test) | `boolean test(T)` | `filter(...)`, `anyMatch`, `allMatch` |
| `Consumer<T>` | T → void (side effect) | `void accept(T)` | `forEach(...)`, `peek(...)` |
| `Supplier<T>` | () → T (produce) | `T get()` | `Stream.generate(...)`, `Optional.orElseGet`, lazy defaults |

These cover most lambda situations. When you need two inputs, use the `Bi*` variants (`BiFunction`, `BiPredicate`, `BiConsumer`). When you need primitive types to avoid boxing, use the specializations (`IntFunction<R>`, `ToIntFunction<T>`, `IntPredicate`, `IntConsumer`, `IntSupplier`).

Mastering these interfaces is what makes Java stream code feel idiomatic — instead of imperative loops with mutable state, you compose pipelines from these named shapes.

sections.title: Function<T, R> — Transformation
Predicate<T> — Testing
Consumer<T> — Side Effects
Supplier<T> — Lazy Production
Two-Argument Variants and Primitive Specializations
Choosing the Right Interface
sections.content:
**Pick by shape**:
- **Need to transform**? `Function<T, R>` (or `UnaryOperator<T>` if T = R).
- **Need to test/filter**? `Predicate<T>`.
- **Need to do something with no return**? `Consumer<T>`.
- **Need to produce a value with no input**? `Supplier<T>`.

**Pick by stream operation**:
- `map` → `Function`.
- `filter` → `Predicate`.
- `forEach`, `peek` → `Consumer`.
- `Stream.generate` → `Supplier`.
- `reduce(identity, op)` → `BinaryOperator`.

**Pick by primitive**:
- Working with primitives in a stream? Use `mapToInt`/`mapToLong`/`mapToDouble` and the primitive interfaces.
- Defining APIs that take primitives? Use `IntFunction`, `IntPredicate`, etc., not the boxed variants.

**Common pitfalls**:
- **Confusing `Function` and `BiFunction`** — read the parameter count.
- **Using `Consumer` to compute a value** — use `Function` instead; `Consumer` returns void.
- **`orElse` vs `orElseGet`** — `orElse` is eager (always evaluated), `orElseGet` is lazy.
- **Boxing in hot paths** — reach for primitive variants.
- **Thrown checked exceptions** — standard interfaces don't declare them; wrap or define a custom interface.
- **Long lambda bodies** — extract to a named method for testability.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Function<T, R>**: T → R, transformation, used in `map`. Method: `apply`. Combinators: `andThen`, `compose`, `identity()`.
- **Predicate<T>**: T → boolean, used in `filter`, `anyMatch`, `allMatch`. Method: `test`. Combinators: `and`, `or`, `negate`, `Predicate.not(...)` (Java 11+).
- **Consumer<T>**: T → void, used in `forEach`, `peek`. Method: `accept`. Combinator: `andThen`.
- **Supplier<T>**: () → T, lazy values, used in `orElseGet`, `Stream.generate`. Method: `get`. No standard combinators.
- **BiFunction**, **BiPredicate**, **BiConsumer** for two inputs.
- **UnaryOperator<T>** = `Function<T, T>`; **BinaryOperator<T>** = `BiFunction<T, T, T>` (used in `reduce`).
- **Primitive specializations**: `IntFunction`, `ToIntFunction`, `IntPredicate`, `IntConsumer`, `IntSupplier`, etc. — avoid boxing.
- **`orElse` vs `orElseGet`**: `orElse` is eager, `orElseGet` is lazy.
- **Use `peek(Consumer)` for debugging**, not for side effects in production pipelines.
- **Compose** with combinators rather than long lambda bodies.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
These four interfaces capture the four basic shapes of computation:

**`Function<T, R>` — transformation**
- Signature: `R apply(T t)` — takes T, returns R
- Used in `map`
- Example: `String::length`, `User::getName`
- Combinators: `andThen` (this then next), `compose` (next then this), `Function.identity()`
- Variants: `BiFunction<T, U, R>`, `UnaryOperator<T>` (T to T), `BinaryOperator<T>` (used in reduce)

**`Predicate<T>` — test**
- Signature: `boolean test(T t)` — takes T, returns boolean
- Used in `filter`, `anyMatch`, `allMatch`, `noneMatch`
- Example: `String::isEmpty`, `User::isActive`
- Combinators: `and`, `or`, `negate`
- Java 11+: `Predicate.not(String::isBlank)` reads better than `s -> !s.isBlank()`

**`Consumer<T>` — side effect**
- Signature: `void accept(T t)` — takes T, returns nothing
- Used in `forEach`, `peek`
- Example: `System.out::println`, `repo::save`
- Combinator: `andThen` (run this then the next)
- Don't abuse — if you find yourself reaching for `forEach` to mutate state, the imperative loop or a proper collector is usually clearer

**`Supplier<T>` — lazy production**
- Signature: `T get()` — takes nothing, returns T
- Used in `Optional.orElseGet`, `Map.computeIfAbsent`, `Stream.generate`, lazy defaults
- Example: `ArrayList::new`, `UUID::randomUUID`
- Critical distinction: `Optional.orElse(expensiveDefault())` calls the default eagerly; `orElseGet(() -> expensiveDefault())` is lazy

**Two-argument variants**
- `BiFunction<T, U, R>`, `BiPredicate<T, U>`, `BiConsumer<T, U>`
- For three or more inputs, define a custom functional interface or use a record/tuple
- `Map.forEach` takes a `BiConsumer<K, V>`

**Primitive specializations — avoid boxing**
- `IntFunction<R>`, `ToIntFunction<T>`, `IntUnaryOperator`, `IntPredicate`, `IntConsumer`, `IntSupplier`
- Same family for `Long` and `Double`
- Use them in hot paths and when the API takes primitives
- Stream pipelines: `.mapToInt(...).sum()` is faster than `.map(...).reduce(0, Integer::sum)` — zero boxing

**How they map to stream operations**
- `map(Function)` — transform
- `filter(Predicate)` — select
- `forEach(Consumer)` — side effect
- `peek(Consumer)` — debugging
- `Stream.generate(Supplier)` — infinite stream
- `reduce(identity, BinaryOperator)` — fold

**Composition examples**
- `Function`: `String::trim` `andThen` `String::toUpperCase` → trim then uppercase
- `Predicate`: `isActive.and(isAdmin)`, `isAdmin.negate()`, `Predicate.not(String::isBlank)`
- `Consumer`: `log.andThen(save)` — log first, then save
- `Supplier`: no built-in combinators — chain manually if needed

**Common pitfalls**
- Confusing `Function` and `BiFunction` — watch the parameter count
- `Consumer` returns void — use `Function` if you need a value back
- `orElse` vs `orElseGet` — eager vs lazy; use `orElseGet` for expensive defaults
- Boxing in hot paths — use primitive specializations
- Checked exceptions — standard interfaces don't declare them; wrap in `RuntimeException` or define a custom interface

**Recommendation:** Memorize these four signatures — they're the foundational vocabulary of modern Java. When designing an API or writing a stream, ask "which shape is this?" — transformation (Function), test (Predicate), side-effect (Consumer), or lazy producer (Supplier) — and pick the matching interface. Use **combinators** (`andThen`, `and`, `or`, `negate`, `Predicate.not`) instead of long lambda bodies; they read better and stay testable. Reach for **primitive specializations** (`IntPredicate`, `ToIntFunction`) in hot paths to avoid GC pressure from boxing. Always prefer **`orElseGet`** over **`orElse`** when the default is expensive to compute. And remember: if your lambda is more than a few lines, extract it to a named method — the symbol gives you a stack trace, a test target, and a place to document intent.

questions.question: What are the four kinds of method references in Java? When do you use each?
questions.title: Method References — The Four Forms and Their Lambda Equivalents
questions.direct_answer: **Method references** (Java 8+) are a compact lambda syntax for the case where the lambda just calls an existing method. The four forms are: **(1) Static method reference** — `ClassName::staticMethod`, e.g., `Integer::parseInt`, equivalent to `s -> Integer.parseInt(s)`; **(2) Bound instance method reference** — `instance::method`, e.g., `System.out::println`, equivalent to `x -> System.out.println(x)`, where the receiver is captured at lambda creation time; **(3) Unbound instance method reference** — `ClassName::instanceMethod`, e.g., `String::toUpperCase`, equivalent to `s -> s.toUpperCase()`, where the first argument becomes the receiver; **(4) Constructor reference** — `ClassName::new`, e.g., `ArrayList::new` (a `Supplier<ArrayList>`), or `User::new` (a `Function<String, User>` for a constructor taking a String). The compiler infers which form based on context and method overloads. Use method references when they read more clearly than the lambda; stick with a lambda when you need parameter rearrangement, multiple operations, or when the method-reference form is ambiguous (multiple matching overloads). Method references are usually slightly more efficient (one less indirection) and signal intent more clearly than a lambda calling one method.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Confusing bound (instance::method) with unbound (Class::method) instance references. Forgetting that `Class::instanceMethod` makes the first argument the receiver. Not knowing constructor references match Supplier or Function based on parameters
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show how method references resolve overloaded methods (compiler picks based on functional interface), explain the bound vs unbound distinction with a concrete example, and discuss when method references can be slightly faster than lambdas (cached call site, no synthetic lambda body)

sections.title: Why Method References Exist
sections.content:
When a lambda's whole job is to call one existing method, **method references** let you skip the parameter list and arrow:

```java
// Lambda — verbose, just delegates to System.out.println
list.forEach(item -> System.out.println(item));

// Method reference — same behavior, less noise
list.forEach(System.out::println);
```

The `::` operator is the method reference syntax. The compiler:
1. Looks at the **target functional interface** (the parameter type expected by `forEach` is `Consumer<T>`).
2. Picks the matching method or overload from the referenced class/object.
3. Wires it up via `LambdaMetafactory`, just like a lambda.

**Benefits**:
- More concise.
- Often more readable (the method name **is** the documentation).
- Slightly more efficient in some cases (one less indirection).
- Encourages naming the operation — if you can name a method, you have a testable unit.

**The four forms** depend on what's being referenced:
1. **Static method**: `ClassName::staticMethod`.
2. **Bound instance method**: `instance::method`.
3. **Unbound instance method**: `ClassName::instanceMethod`.
4. **Constructor**: `ClassName::new`.

sections.content:
**Common pitfalls**:
- **Confusing bound and unbound**: `instance::method` (bound, no-arg lambda) vs `Class::method` (unbound, takes one arg).
- **Ambiguous overloads**: `System.out::println` works because there's a `println(String)` and `println(Object)`; the compiler picks based on the functional interface. If multiple overloads match, you may need a lambda for explicit disambiguation.
- **`null` receiver in bound reference**: `nullThing::method` throws NPE at the moment the method reference is created (Java evaluates the receiver eagerly).
- **Capturing mutable receiver**: bound reference to `instance::method` captures the instance reference, but if `instance` is mutable, behavior could change later.
- **Overload disambiguation**: if a class has overloaded methods, the compiler picks based on the target functional interface signature. If none match, you get a compile error; if multiple match, ambiguity error.

**Style guidelines**:
- Prefer method references when they read clearly: `User::getName`.
- Stick with lambdas when you need transformation: `u -> u.getName().toUpperCase()`.
- Avoid method references that obscure intent (e.g., a static utility with a non-obvious name).
- Method references with generic methods sometimes need explicit type witnesses: `<String>compareTo` etc., but this is rare.

**Refactoring tip**:
- IDEs (IntelliJ, Eclipse) suggest converting `x -> someMethod(x)` to a method reference. Generally accept these unless the lambda is doing something non-trivial.

sections.content:
- **Four forms** of method references:
  - **Static**: `ClassName::staticMethod` — `Integer::parseInt`.
  - **Bound instance**: `instance::method` — `System.out::println`. Receiver fixed at creation.
  - **Unbound instance**: `ClassName::instanceMethod` — `String::toUpperCase`. First lambda arg is the receiver.
  - **Constructor**: `ClassName::new` — `ArrayList::new`. Matches Supplier or Function/BiFunction by parameter count.
- **Bound vs unbound** is the most common source of confusion: bound captures the receiver; unbound makes the first arg the receiver.
- **Compiler infers the target functional interface** from context and resolves the matching method/overload.
- **Use method references** when the lambda body is just a method call; lambdas otherwise.
- **Performance**: usually as fast or marginally faster; non-capturing static references are cached.
- **Constructor references** match `Supplier<T>` (no-arg constructor) or `Function/BiFunction` based on parameter count.
- **Array constructor**: `String[]::new` is `IntFunction<String[]>` for `stream.toArray(...)`.
- **`null` receiver** in bound reference fails at creation time (eager evaluation).
- **Pitfalls**: ambiguous overloads, mistaking bound for unbound, mutable captured receiver.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Method references are a compact lambda syntax for the case where the lambda just calls an existing method. The `::` operator separates the type/instance from the method name. There are four forms:

**1. Static method reference — `ClassName::staticMethod`**
- Refers to a static method of a class
- Example: `Integer::parseInt`, equivalent to `s -> Integer.parseInt(s)`
- Other examples: `Math::max`, `Objects::requireNonNull`, `String::valueOf`
- Lambda parameters become method arguments, in order

**2. Bound instance method reference — `instance::method`**
- Receiver is captured at the moment the reference is created
- Example: `System.out::println`, equivalent to `s -> System.out.println(s)`
- The `System.out` PrintStream is captured; lambda parameters are method arguments
- Other examples: `userRepo::save`, `cache::get`, `logger::error`
- Be careful: if the receiver is null at creation time, you get NPE immediately

**3. Unbound instance method reference — `ClassName::instanceMethod`**
- The **first lambda parameter** becomes the receiver
- Example: `String::toUpperCase`, equivalent to `s -> s.toUpperCase()`
- BiFunction example: `String::equalsIgnoreCase` is `(a, b) -> a.equalsIgnoreCase(b)` — first arg is receiver, second is method argument
- Common in stream maps: `User::getName`, `Order::getTotal`

**4. Constructor reference — `ClassName::new`**
- Refers to a constructor; the compiler picks the overload by parameter count
- `ArrayList::new` is a `Supplier<ArrayList>` for the no-arg constructor
- `User::new` could match `Function<String, User>` for `User(String)` or `BiFunction<String, String, User>` for `User(String, String)`
- Array constructor: `String[]::new` is `IntFunction<String[]>` for `stream.toArray(...)`

**Bound vs unbound — the trickiest distinction**

```java
String s = "hello";
Supplier<Integer> bound = s::length;       // s captured, no args
Function<String, Integer> unbound = String::length;  // arg becomes receiver
```

- **Bound**: looks like `instance::method` — receiver fixed
- **Unbound**: looks like `Class::method` and `method` is an instance method — first arg is receiver
- **Static**: looks like `Class::method` and `method` is a static method

The compiler disambiguates based on whether the method is static and what target functional interface is expected.

**Lambda vs method reference — when to use which**

**Use method reference when**:
- The lambda just calls one method
- The method name is self-documenting
- Common cases: `User::getName`, `Objects::nonNull`, `String::isEmpty`, `System.out::println`

**Use lambda when**:
- You need to rearrange parameters
- You need multiple operations
- You need to add a constant
- The method-reference form is ambiguous

**Performance**
- Method references are usually as fast or marginally faster than lambdas
- Non-capturing static and unbound references are cached — zero allocation per call
- Bound references capture the receiver — one allocation per capture (small cost)
- Constructor references in hot paths: watch allocation; usually fine

**Pitfalls**
- **Bound vs unbound confusion** — the most common interview trap
- **Ambiguous overloads** — if multiple methods match the target signature, the compiler errors out; sometimes you need a lambda for explicit disambiguation
- **`null` receiver in bound reference** — NPE at creation time; the receiver is evaluated eagerly
- **Mutable captured receiver** — bound reference holds the instance reference; if it mutates, behavior changes

**Recommendation:** Use method references **as the default** when the lambda just calls one method — they read better, document intent, and are sometimes faster. Stick with **lambdas** when you need parameter rearrangement, multiple operations, or to add constants. The trickiest case is bound vs unbound — remember the rule: `instance::method` is bound (receiver fixed), `Class::method` on an instance method is unbound (first arg becomes receiver). For constructor references, the compiler picks the overload by parameter count, so `User::new` can be a `Supplier`, a `Function`, or a `BiFunction` depending on context. Trust your IDE's hints — IntelliJ and Eclipse will suggest converting `x -> foo(x)` to `this::foo` or `MyClass::foo` automatically; usually accept those unless the lambda was doing something non-trivial.

questions.title: Java Streams API — How It Works and Most Useful Operations
questions.question: How do Java Streams work, and what are the most useful stream operations?
questions.direct_answer: A **Stream** is a **lazy pipeline** from a source through intermediate operations to a terminal operation. It's not a data structure — it holds no elements; it pulls from a source on demand. **Intermediate operations** (`filter`, `map`, `flatMap`, `distinct`, `sorted`, `limit`, `skip`, `peek`) return a new stream and defer execution. **Terminal operations** (`collect`, `forEach`, `reduce`, `count`, `findFirst`, `anyMatch`, `toArray`) trigger execution and consume the stream. The most-used operations in production: **`filter` + `map` + `collect(toList())`** as the basic pattern, **`groupingBy` with downstream collectors** for aggregation, **`flatMap`** for un-nesting, **`reduce`** for folds, and **`findFirst`** combined with short-circuiting for early termination. Streams shine for multi-step transformations and aggregation but aren't always faster than loops — use them when they communicate intent better.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Treating streams like collections (reusing after terminal op); using parallel stream by default; writing six-line pipelines where a for loop would be clearer
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain laziness + short-circuiting combining to avoid work; mention that streams are one-shot; cite the NQ rule for parallel-stream decisions

sections.title: Streams = Lazy Pipelines
sections.content:
The key insight about streams: a `Stream<T>` is **not a data structure**. It holds no elements. It's a **pipeline** of operations that pulls elements from a source on demand and processes them in order.

A `List<T>` is a data structure — you can query its size, read elements by index, iterate multiple times. A `Stream<T>` is a recipe — you describe what should happen to elements as they flow through, and the pipeline executes **once** when a terminal operation triggers it.

This lazy, one-shot design enables two critical optimizations:

1. **Lazy evaluation** — intermediate operations don't run until the terminal operation demands data. `stream.filter(...).map(...)` by itself does nothing.
2. **Short-circuiting** — terminal operations like `findFirst`, `anyMatch`, `limit(n)` can stop the pipeline as soon as they have their answer. Elements past the stopping point are never examined.

Together, these let `users.stream().filter(User::isActive).findFirst()` on a list of 10 million users examine only a handful of elements — the pipeline stops at the first active user.

Every stream pipeline has exactly **three parts**:

```
source  →  zero or more intermediates  →  exactly one terminal
```

Miss the terminal and nothing runs. Add a second terminal and you get `IllegalStateException: stream has already been operated upon`.

sections.title: The Most-Used Operations in Practice
Laziness + Short-Circuiting — Why Streams Are Fast
sections.content:
The theoretical appeal of streams is pretty code. The practical appeal is that **lazy evaluation combined with short-circuiting** produces efficient execution.

**Example**: finding the first completed order in a large list.

```java
Order found = orders.stream()         // 10 million orders
    .filter(o -> o.getStatus() == COMPLETED)
    .findFirst()
    .orElseThrow();
```

What actually happens:

1. `findFirst()` pulls one element from the upstream `filter`
2. `filter` pulls one element from `orders.stream()`
3. If the element satisfies the predicate, `filter` emits it; `findFirst` wraps it in `Optional` and returns
4. If not, `filter` pulls the next element and checks again

**Only elements up to the first completed order are examined**. If the first order in the list is completed, only one element is processed. If the first 1,000 are pending and #1,001 is completed, 1,001 elements are processed. The 8,999,000 elements after that are never touched.

Without laziness, `filter` would eagerly evaluate all 10 million elements and build a new list, then `findFirst` would take the first — massive wasted work.

**Short-circuit terminals**:
- `findFirst()`, `findAny()` — stop at first match
- `anyMatch(p)`, `allMatch(p)`, `noneMatch(p)` — stop at first decisive element
- `limit(n)` (as a short-circuit intermediate) — stop after n elements

**Ordering the pipeline for efficiency**:

```java
// GOOD: cheap filter first, expensive operation only on survivors
orders.stream()
    .filter(Order::isCompleted)          // cheap
    .map(this::enrichWithCustomerData)   // expensive (DB lookup)
    .collect(toList());

// BAD: expensive operation on every order, then most discarded
orders.stream()
    .map(this::enrichWithCustomerData)   // expensive — runs on all
    .filter(Order::isCompleted)          // most filtered away
    .collect(toList());
```

A one-line reorder can be 10x speedup — the cheap `filter` is a fraction of the expensive `map`'s cost.

sections.title: When Streams Help — and When They Hurt
sections.content:
**Streams are excellent for**:
- Multi-step transformation chains (3+ steps) — pipeline reads top-to-bottom
- Grouping, partitioning, and statistical aggregation (`groupingBy`, `summarizingInt`)
- Operations naturally expressing intent (`anyMatch`, `findFirst`, `count`)
- Lazy + short-circuit opportunities on large sources

**Streams hurt when**:

- **Simple single-step loops** — `for (x : list) process(x)` is clearer than `list.forEach(this::process)`
- **Index-aware logic** — streams don't expose indices naturally. Use `IntStream.range(0, list.size()).forEach(...)` as a workaround, or just use `for`.
- **Checked exceptions in lambdas** — `stream.map(Files::readString)` doesn't compile (`IOException`). Workaround: wrap in try-catch (ugly) or use a library like `jOOλ`.
- **Mutable shared state** — `forEach` with mutation works but is an anti-pattern; use `reduce` or `collect` instead.
- **Performance-critical primitive loops** — raw `for` loops on `int[]` can beat streams by 10-30% due to no boxing/unboxing. Use `IntStream` over `int[]` to close the gap.

**Parallel streams** deserve a separate caution: they don't automatically make your code faster.

- All parallel streams share `ForkJoinPool.commonPool()` — `cores - 1` threads
- Use only when: ArrayList/array source, substantial per-element work (microseconds+), no shared mutable state, no I/O blocking
- Doug Lea's NQ rule: parallelize when `elements × work-per-element > ~10,000`
- **Never** run blocking I/O on a parallel stream — starves the common pool

**2026 recommendation** with Java 21+: prefer **virtual threads** over parallel streams for I/O-bound work. `Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()` gives you concurrency without the common-pool trap.

**Readability heuristic**: if the stream pipeline is longer than ~5 lines or has nested `flatMap`s, extract helper methods or rewrite as a `for` loop. Shorter is not always clearer.

sections.content:
- **Stream = lazy pipeline**, not a data structure. Source, intermediates, terminal.
- **Intermediate**: `filter`, `map`, `flatMap`, `distinct`, `sorted`, `limit`, `skip`, `peek` — lazy.
- **Terminal**: `collect`, `forEach`, `reduce`, `count`, `findFirst`, `anyMatch`, `toArray` — eager.
- **One-shot** — can't traverse a stream twice; throws `IllegalStateException`.
- **Laziness + short-circuiting** lets `findFirst` examine only a few elements from a 10M-element source.
- **Order pipeline for efficiency**: cheap filters before expensive maps.
- **`Collectors.groupingBy` with downstream collectors** covers most aggregation needs.
- **Parallel streams** rarely help — use only when ArrayList source + substantial work per element + no blocking I/O.
- **Java 16+**: `stream.toList()` replaces `stream.collect(toList())` and returns unmodifiable list.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
A **Stream** is a **lazy pipeline**, not a data structure. It pulls elements from a source — a `List`, array, generator, or I/O channel — and pushes them through a chain of operations.

Every pipeline has three parts: **source**, **zero or more intermediate operations**, and **exactly one terminal operation**.

**Intermediate operations** — `filter`, `map`, `flatMap`, `distinct`, `sorted`, `limit`, `skip`, `peek` — return another stream and are **lazy**. Nothing executes until a terminal operation is attached.

**Terminal operations** — `collect`, `forEach`, `reduce`, `count`, `findFirst`, `anyMatch`, `toArray` — trigger execution and consume the stream.

The **most-used pattern in production** is `stream().filter(...).map(...).collect(toList())` — the Stream API's equivalent of SQL's SELECT with WHERE. For aggregation, `Collectors.groupingBy` with a **downstream collector** — like `groupingBy(Order::getStatus, counting())` — is dramatically more expressive than manual loops.

The **why** of lazy evaluation is performance via **short-circuiting**. `orders.stream().filter(Order::isCompleted).findFirst()` on 10 million orders may examine only the first few — `findFirst` stops as soon as it has its answer, and `filter` only processes what `findFirst` requests. Without laziness, every element would be filtered eagerly before `findFirst` got a chance.

**A practical tip**: order the pipeline so cheap operations come before expensive ones. `filter(isCompleted).map(this::enrichFromDatabase)` is 10x faster than `map(this::enrichFromDatabase).filter(isCompleted)` — the cheap filter avoids the database lookups for elements you'll discard.

A couple of **gotchas** worth knowing. Streams are **one-shot** — after a terminal op, you can't reuse them; throws `IllegalStateException`. If you need multiple traversals, either collect to a `List` first or wrap in a `Supplier<Stream<T>>`. And **parallel streams** — `parallelStream()` — are rarely the answer they look like. They share the common ForkJoinPool, can starve on blocking I/O, and only help when the per-element work times the element count exceeds about 10,000. For I/O-bound parallelism on **Java 21**, virtual threads are almost always the better choice.

questions.title: Optional Proper Usage — Return Types, orElse, and Anti-Patterns
questions.question: How should you use Java Optional correctly, and what are the common anti-patterns?
questions.direct_answer: **`Optional<T>`** was designed as a **return type** for methods where absence is a normal outcome — to force callers to handle the empty case. Per Brian Goetz (Java language architect), it was **not** intended as a general null replacement. Use it on method **return types**; **avoid** it as field types, method parameters, or collection elements. The idiomatic way to consume an `Optional` is through **`map`**, **`filter`**, **`orElse`**, **`orElseGet`**, **`orElseThrow`**, and **`ifPresent`** — **never** `isPresent()` followed by `get()` (that's null-checking in disguise). The single most common bug: **`orElse`** always evaluates its argument, so `opt.orElse(computeExpensive())` computes the expensive value even when the Optional is present. Use **`orElseGet(supplier)`** for lazy evaluation. And remember: `Optional` is **not `Serializable`** — it breaks on JPA entities and DTOs that cross serialization boundaries.

sections.title: Optional Is for Return Types — Not Everywhere
sections.content:
`Optional<T>` is among the most **misused** features in the Java standard library. It was introduced in Java 8 with a narrow, specific purpose.

Brian Goetz, Java's language architect, has said:

> "Optional was added to Java to address a specific problem: the return value of functions that may or may not have a value. It was not intended to be a general-purpose `Maybe` type."

The intent: when a method might return nothing, its return type should **force the caller to think about the absent case**. `Optional<User> findByEmail(String email)` makes absence obvious. `User findByEmail(String email)` (where `null` means absent) relies on convention and memory — easy to forget.

The **wrong** uses that developers adopt anyway:

- **`Optional` fields on JPA entities** — not `Serializable`; JPA doesn't know how to map it; wastes an allocation per field.
- **`Optional` method parameters** — forces the caller to wrap with `Optional.of(x)` or `Optional.empty()`, which is worse than passing `null` or overloading methods.
- **`Optional` elements in collections** — `List<Optional<String>>` is almost always better as a filtered `List<String>`.
- **Wrapping a nullable reference at every layer** — creates `Optional<Optional<T>>`-style monstrosities.

The practical rule: `Optional` on return types where absence is possible; **not** anywhere else.

sections.content:
- **Optional = return type** for methods where absence is possible — not fields, parameters, or collection elements.
- **Not `Serializable`** — breaks on JPA entities and network-serialized DTOs.
- **Idiomatic consumption**: `map`, `flatMap`, `filter`, `ifPresent`/`ifPresentOrElse`, `orElse`/`orElseGet`/`orElseThrow`.
- **Avoid `isPresent() + get()`** — you just reinvented null-checking.
- **`orElse` vs `orElseGet`**: `orElse` always evaluates; `orElseGet` is lazy. Use `orElse` only for literal defaults.
- **`flatMap`** avoids `Optional<Optional<T>>`.
- **Primitive specializations** (`OptionalInt`, `OptionalLong`, `OptionalDouble`) avoid boxing.
- **Java 9+**: `Optional.stream()` to bridge to Stream; `Optional.or(Supplier)` for lazy fallback chains; `ifPresentOrElse(action, emptyAction)` for both cases.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
`Optional<T>` is one of the most **misused** features in the Java standard library. Per Brian Goetz, the Java language architect, it was designed specifically as a **return type** for methods where absence is possible — to force callers to think about the empty case. It was **not** intended as a general null replacement.

The correct use is on **method return types**. The incorrect uses I see everywhere: `Optional` fields on JPA entities (breaks serialization), `Optional` method parameters (caller must wrap/unwrap awkwardly — overload methods instead), and `Optional` inside collections (filter nulls first or use a `Map` for sparse data).

For **consuming** an `Optional`, the idiomatic operations are **`map`**, **`flatMap`**, **`filter`**, **`ifPresent`** and **`ifPresentOrElse`** (Java 9+), and the three 'extract' operations: **`orElse`**, **`orElseGet`**, **`orElseThrow`**. **Avoid `isPresent()` followed by `get()`** — that's null-checking with a wrapper, which defeats the design.

The single most common production bug: **confusing `orElse` and `orElseGet`**. `orElse(T)` takes a value and **always evaluates it**. So `opt.orElse(expensiveCall())` runs `expensiveCall()` every single time, even when the `Optional` is present. `orElseGet(Supplier<T>)` is lazy — only calls the supplier when the `Optional` is empty. **Rule: `orElse` for literal defaults, `orElseGet` for anything requiring computation.** I've debugged real production slowdowns where a 50ms remote call was baked into an endpoint via `orElse`, running on every request whether needed or not.

Two **Java 9+ features** worth knowing. **`Optional.stream()`** bridges `Optional` to `Stream` — `.flatMap(Optional::stream)` filters out empties in a stream of Optionals. **`or(Supplier<Optional<T>>)`** chains fallback sources lazily — `primary.or(() -> secondary).or(() -> cache)`. Each fallback is called only if needed.

**Final rule**: keep `Optional` in its intended lane — method return types — and it makes code clearer. Extend it beyond that and it obscures intent, adds overhead, and breaks serialization.
